title: Mosh, Glass, Elastic Type, Morphs & Interest
description: Codec-feedback datamosh, a canvas layer over live DOM, letters on an animated bezier, spring icon morphing, and interestfor hover cards.

drops.title: Datamosh Feedback
drops.description: Each frame is the previous frame warped by block motion vectors, with only a sliver of fresh render blended back in.
drops.concept: Codrops published a real-time datamosh built on the decoder formula 'new frame = warp(previous frame, motion vectors) + residual'. This drop reimplements it in Canvas 2D: three tiles run their own scene, a velocity field is stamped per moving shape, then one quantised motion vector per macroblock drags the previous frame's pixels around while a small residual leaks the fresh render back in. Skip thresholds freeze still blocks, lost sectors suppress motion, and dragging injects gesture motion that fades over ~370 ms.
drops.source: Niccolò Fanton — 'Breaking the Frame: Building a Real-Time Datamosh Effect with Three.js' on Codrops

interaction.mouse: Drag inside any tile to inject motion into the velocity field and start the smear.
interaction.click: Tune block size, motion gain, residual and lost-sector rate; 'Force keyframe' resets the history buffers.
interaction.touch: Single-finger drag does the same as a mouse drag; the panel stacks above the tiles on small screens.

drops.title: Live DOM Under Glass
drops.description: A canvas effect layer sits on top of a real bento grid — text still selects, links still click, the input still focuses.
drops.concept: HTML-in-Canvas, in origin trial from Chrome 148, lets drawElementImage() render a live DOM element into a 2D, WebGL or WebGPU context — the element stays in the DOM, keeps its layout, its place in the accessibility tree and its events, while its pixels become yours to distort. Everywhere else the honest posture is an overlay, and that is what this drop builds: a real bento grid in normal flow with a pointer-events:none canvas layered over it in screen blend mode. Ripple, lens and dither modes track the pointer through the stage element rather than the canvas, and on-page counters prove the links and text field underneath are still live.
drops.source: 'Introducing the HTML-in-Canvas API origin trial' on Chrome for Developers

interaction.mouse: Move over the grid to drive the effect; select text and click the links to prove the DOM is untouched.
interaction.click: Switch between Ripple, Lens and Dither, and tune radius, strength and speed.
interaction.touch: Drag to move the effect origin; the grid collapses to two columns and the panel moves inline.

drops.title: Elastic Path Type
drops.description: Every letter rides the same animated bezier via offset-path: shape(), distributed by sibling-index().
drops.concept: A CSS-only elastic text effect that puts each letter on a shared shape() path and spaces them with sibling-index()/sibling-count(). A single registered @property animates the curve's two control points from flat to arched, and an elastic linear() easing gives the word its snap. This build adds a calc() arch fallback for engines without shape(), sets --i/--n from script so the maths holds either way, and keeps an aria-label on each link so per-letter splitting does not destroy the accessible name.
drops.source: 'How to Create a CSS-only Elastic Text Effect' on blog.master.dev

interaction.mouse: Hover any word — the whole line arcs along the curve and springs back on leave.
interaction.click: Adjust curve height, duration, arc direction and easing; the panel reports which native features the browser has.
interaction.touch: Tap a word to trigger the arc; three words loop the effect on their own so it reads without hover.

drops.title: Icon Morph Spring
drops.description: Any stroke icon becomes any other — 64-point resampling, a Procrustes fit, and a 240 Hz damped spring.
drops.concept: Morphicons morphs arbitrary stroke icons into each other by resampling both outlines to 64 arc-length-equidistant points, running a 2D Procrustes fit to recover the rotation and scale that best align them, then interpolating similarity and residual separately so shapes never collapse in transit. This reimplementation does the same with nine hand-generated outlines, searches for the index offset that stops the loops twisting, and drives progress with a damped harmonic oscillator stepped at 240 Hz — retargeting freezes the on-screen shape and keeps the velocity, so spam-tapping stays fluid.
drops.source: guillermolg00/morphicons — universal morphing for stroke-based icons with spring physics

interaction.mouse: Click the large icon to advance the cycle, or any pill to toggle its pair; drag the scrubber for controlled mode.
interaction.click: Pick a spring preset or dial stiffness, damping and auto-cycle speed; the panel reports the fitted θ and σ.
interaction.touch: Tap targets are 74 px pills; interrupting a morph mid-flight keeps its velocity instead of snapping.

drops.title: Interest Cards
drops.description: Hover cards with no hover JavaScript — interestfor points a trigger at a popover and the browser owns the timing.
drops.concept: The Interest Invoker API replaces bespoke tooltip logic with a single declarative signal that fires for hover, keyboard focus and long-press alike. A trigger carries interestfor, the target is any popover, and interest-show-delay / interest-hide-delay move the feel into CSS. This drop wires four rich cards into running prose, styles the :has-interest states, animates entry with @starting-style, and ships a fallback that reproduces the same semantics — delays, long-press, escape-to-close — where the API has not landed yet.
drops.source: 'A First Look at the Interest Invoker API (for Hover-Triggered Popovers)' on CSS-Tricks

interaction.mouse: Hover any dashed link to raise its card after the show delay; move away and it retracts after the hide delay.
interaction.click: Drag the two delay sliders to feel the difference between eager and deliberate; the log shows each interest event.
interaction.touch: Long-press a link to signal interest, tap elsewhere or press Escape to dismiss.
